reason: The provided sources contain more than 10 double-sourced facts supporting a compelling, fast-paced story with a remarkable central twist.
story: On July 28, 1945, Lieutenant Colonel William F. Smith Jr. flew a B-25 toward Newark in heavy fog. The aircraft struck the Empire State Building at more than 200 miles per hour, damaging the 78th and 79th floors. One engine fell down an elevator shaft. Elevator operator Betty Lou Oliver survived a 75-floor elevator plunge but suffered serious fractures. The checked institutional archive documents her survival without establishing an air-cushion mechanism. Contemporary accounts differ on the exact sequence of her rescue and fall.
angle: Elevator operator Betty Lou Oliver survived a 75-story plunge into the basement after severed cables sent her elevator falling from the 80th floor.

claims.claim: On July 28, 1945, a US Army B-25 Mitchell bomber crashed into the Empire State Building in New York City.
The bomber was piloted by Lieutenant Colonel William F. Smith Jr. on a flight originating from Massachusetts.
Thick fog over Manhattan reduced visibility to near zero and disoriented the pilot.
The plane narrowly missed the Chrysler Building on 42nd Street before turning right into Midtown skyscrapers.
The aircraft struck the north side of the Empire State Building between the 78th and 80th floors at over 200 miles per hour.
The collision tore an 18-by-20-foot hole in the building structure.
The crash killed 14 people, consisting of three crewmen on the aircraft and eleven civilians in the building.
One engine shot completely through the building and landed on a roof a block away on 33rd Street.
One engine fell down an elevator shaft; the precise relation to elevator cable failure is disputed across accounts.
claims.confidence: high for engine fall; cable sequence disputed

claims.claim: Elevator operator Betty Lou Oliver survived a 75-floor fall inside an elevator car; accounts differ on the rescue and cable sequence.
claims.confidence: high for survival and fall; sequence disputed

claims.claim: An air-cushion explanation for Oliver’s survival appears in weaker secondary retellings but is not established by the checked NYC archive or NPR reporting; do not state it as fact.
Oliver suffered a broken pelvis, back, and neck from the crash landing in the subbasement.
New York firefighters brought the high-altitude structural fire under control within 40 minutes.
Office worker Therese Fortier Willig threw her rings out a 79th-floor window while trapped by fire.
Despite the destruction, the Empire State Building reopened for business on many floors less than 48 hours later.
The disaster spurred the passage of the Federal Tort Claims Act of 1946, enabling citizens to sue the US government.

disputed: The exact time of impact varies across sources (S1 and S7 cite 9:40 a.m., S3 and S6 cite approximately 9:50 a.m.); scripts should use a general phrase like 'shortly before 10:00 a.m.'
The estimated speed of the bomber differs slightly (S3 and S7 cite 200 mph, S5 estimates 400 kph / 250 mph); scripts should state 'over 200 miles per hour.'

Impact location details vary slightly (S1 and S7 cite 78th to 80th floors, S2 and S5 cite the 79th floor, S3 and S6 cite 78th and 79th floors); scripts should describe the impact across floors 78 to 80.

The air-cushion explanation is not established by NYC Municipal Archives or NPR and must not be narrated as cause. Sources also differ on whether Oliver was already in the elevator or placed there after initial injury; avoid a specific transfer sequence.
